doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

title: How he composed and his deadline schedule
summary: Watching his father sketch themes, his Bartok influence, Skullduggery and Afrique, and the all-night writing before conducting on a Universal soundstage.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yes it is. Were you witness to, I guess I’m wondering, because he did so much and you know he’d had these assignments. How did he conceive of new themes? Did you ever witness —

I actually witnessed a couple of times, especially with the television stuff, he was doing an “Ironside” once and there was a race theme in there. And we’re sitting in the pool. He kept a little piece of that and he was thinking about [scats] and he said, you know I’ve got an idea for this. And he scribbles it out, because he had perfect pitch so he knew exactly

what he was writing all the time. And he came up with some pretty creative stuff. Plus he was influenced by a lot of the great classical composers. He did a solo on “All the Way” and I was trying to think if it was Moodsville was one of his early Prestige albums. And Bartok’s Concerto for Orchestra, I can’t remember the movement [scats]. Well he started his cadenza with that. He changed keys, he did all kind of different — and when I first heard it I said, “That’s Bartok.” But he was very influenced by a lot of those guys. So he would take a lot of time to come up with different stuff. And I think the Hollywood stuff really helped him because he did a movie called “Skullduggery” with a young Burt Reynolds. It was not a great movie. But he had to think of some ideas because this was about the missing link in Australia [scats]. And he wrote a tune called “Afrique” with Count Basie and he actually used that theme and made a tune out of it.
Aha. He must have always been thinking about something musical I would guess.

Always. But you know what? The interesting thing about Dad was kind of like me, if you gave him four weeks for a show, he would never start on it four weeks before. He always did his most creative stuff when he was under the gun. Sometimes he would write 16, 17 hours. I’d try to stay up with him, it’s four o’clock in the morning and he’s finishing up because he never allowed anybody to orchestrate. He did all that stuff himself. So he would come up with the stuff, write it out, he was very meticulous and very thorough about how he lined his paper, everything. So five o’clock in the morning he’s finishing the last score for a scene. We’d drive to Universal Studios, because this was before emails and sending files, drop it off, go back home, take a shower. The copyists have got it by six, and at eight o’clock the musicians are sitting on the soundstage and he’s got to conduct all day.
Oh, so it was a really pretty tough schedule. And he learned that you’re no better than your producer. If your producer does not like you you’re done.
